rejected.title: Country and landforms
card: For First Nations Australians, Country/Place takes in landforms, waters, sky, plants, animals and people, all connected. It is far more than land.
A landform such as a hill, waterhole or reef is part of Country/Place, not separate scenery. People belong to it and have duties to care for it.
Aboriginal Dreaming stories and Torres Strait Islander Creation stories explain how the land, waters and landforms came to be.
The stories also carry law and knowledge, such as how to behave, how to care for places and where to find water. They are passed on through generations.
rejected.remember: Landforms are part of Country/Place, and the stories about them also hold law and knowledge.

a.q: Why are landforms seen as part of Country/Place, not just scenery?
opts: They are connected to people, law and stories
They are too remote for most people to visit
They belong to whoever holds the land title
They are protected inside national parks
a.why: Country/Place joins landforms with people, waters, living things and the stories that carry law. Being in a national park or on titled land is about how land is managed, not about this connection.

b.q: An Elder explains how a range of hills was made by Ancestral Beings. The same story says who may visit the hills and when. What does this show about the story?
opts: It explains the land and also carries law
It is about the past and holds no rules today
It explains the land but not how to behave
It only describes what the hills look like
b.why: The story tells how the hills came to be, and it also sets out who may visit them and when, which is law. The option saying it explains the land but not how to behave misses the second part of the story.
b.clue: Look at both things the story does.

version.title: Country and landforms
card: For First Nations Australians, Country/Place takes in the land, waters, sky, plants, animals and people, all connected to each other.
Landforms such as hills, rivers, waterholes and reefs are part of Country/Place, not separate scenery. People belong to Country and have a duty to care for it.
Aboriginal Dreaming stories and Torres Strait Islander Creation stories tell how the land, sea and landforms were made, often by Ancestral Beings.
The stories also carry law and knowledge, such as how to behave, how to care for places and where to find water and food. They are passed down through generations and still guide people today.
version.remember: The stories that explain how landforms were made also carry law and knowledge.

a.q: Which describes a landform as part of Country/Place?
opts: A waterhole linked to people, stories and law
A waterhole valued only for the water it holds
A waterhole that is just scenery for visitors
A waterhole owned by whoever fenced it first
a.why: Country/Place connects land, waters, living things and people, and the stories that carry law. Valuing a waterhole only for its water treats it as a resource on its own, apart from those connections.

b.q: A student says Aboriginal Dreaming stories only explain how the land was made. What has the student left out?
opts: They also carry law and knowledge for today
They are mainly about plants, not landforms
They describe the sky and stars, not the land
They belong to the tourists who visit the sites
b.why: Dreaming stories do explain how the land was made, but they also carry law and knowledge, such as how to behave and how to care for places, and they still guide people. The options about plants or the sky are wrong, because the stories do explain landforms.
b.clue: Stories can do more than one thing.

a.best: A waterhole linked to people, stories and law

b.best: They also carry law and knowledge for today

problems.detail: The question asks what the student has left out, and only the right option is an addition (its word "also" answers "only" directly). The three wrong options replace or contradict the claim rather than add to it, so a student could pick the right one from the grammar alone. Wrong options that each name something the stories could plausibly add (for example, that they are only about animals, or only for ceremonies long ago) would test the idea better.

check.summary: The facts and both right answers are sound. Question b's wording gives its answer away, because only the right option is something the student left out; the point is also about First Nations cultures, so it needs the owner's review.
